n: After twenty years of building — seven for the temple and thirteen for his palace — Solomon turned to other projects across his kingdom.
Solomon rebuilt cities that Huram had given (or returned) to him and settled Israelites there. 1 Kings says Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities; perhaps Hiram, displeased, gave them back.

f.w: the cities which Huram had restored to Solomon

n: Solomon conquered Hamath-zobah, an area in Syria — his only recorded military campaign.

f.g: A region of Aramean (Syrian) territory north of Israel.

n: He built Tadmor, a desert oasis on the trade routes, and store cities in the Hamath region to secure trade and supplies.

f.g: Later known as Palmyra, an oasis in the Syrian desert.
Towns for storing grain, supplies, and equipment.

n: Solomon fortified Upper and Lower Beth-horon, guarding a key pass from the coast up to Jerusalem.

f.g: Heavy bolts to secure the gates.

n: He also built Baalath, more store and chariot cities, and whatever else he wanted in Jerusalem, Lebanon, and throughout his realm.
The Chronicler names the remnants of Canaan’s earlier inhabitants still living in the land.

f.w: the Hittites, and the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites

n: Solomon conscripted these remaining non-Israelite peoples into forced labor, which continued to the Chronicler’s source’s time.
Israelites were not made slaves; they served as soldiers, commanders, and officers. (1 Kings 5 does record Israelites being drafted for rotating labor, which later caused resentment.)

f.w: of the children of Israel did Solomon make no servants

n: Two hundred fifty chief officials supervised the work and the workers.
Solomon moved his Egyptian wife, Pharaoh’s daughter, out of David’s palace because places where the ark had been were holy. This hints at tension: a foreign, likely idolatrous wife near holy things.
Solomon offered burnt offerings on the Lord’s altar in front of the temple porch.
He followed Moses’ law exactly: daily offerings, Sabbath and new-moon offerings, and the three yearly pilgrim festivals — Unleavened Bread (Passover), Weeks (Pentecost), and Tabernacles.

f.w: after a certain rate every day

n: He also organized priests, Levites, and gatekeepers in their rotating divisions, exactly as David had ordained. The Chronicler loves to show worship done in order.

f.g: A title usually given to prophets; here it honors David’s inspired arrangements.

n: The priests and Levites followed the king’s instructions faithfully in every matter, including the treasuries.
All Solomon’s work, from laying the foundation to completion, was carried out, and the temple was finished.
Solomon went to the Red Sea ports of Ezion-geber and Eloth (Elath) in Edom’s territory.

f.g: A port at the northern tip of the Gulf of Aqaba.

n: Huram sent ships and skilled Phoenician sailors who, together with Solomon’s men, sailed to Ophir and brought back 450 talents of gold — over 15 tons.
